sentences.text: Hauffiopteryx was a relatively small ichthyosaur that grew to lengths between 2 and 3 meters.
The lectotype specimen of this species measures approximately 1.93 meters in length.
It possessed a short, very thin snout that tapered to a sharp point.
The tooth crowns featured smooth outer surfaces, with the rear teeth being larger than the front ones.
The eye sockets of Hauffiopteryx typicus were notably large and circular.
Strongly forked dorsal ribs at their upper ends gave the skeleton a distinct double-headed appearance.
Each forelimb had four main digits, with some elements on the front edge featuring indentations.
Unlike the forelimbs, each hindlimb possessed only three main digits.
The type specimen is an articulated complete skeleton that preserved the skull and some soft tissues.
Additional materials from England are all juveniles or infants that preserved nearly the entire skeleton and some skulls.
Michael W. Maisch originally described Hauffiopteryx based on specimens previously referred to Stenopterygius hauffianus.
Friedrich von Huene originally recognized Hauffiopteryx in 1931 as a subspecies of S. hauffianus named Stenopterygius hauffianus typica.
Michael W. Maisch elevated it to species rank and reassigned it to its own genus, Hauffiopteryx, in 2008.
Additional materials were described by Hannah Caine and Michael J. Benton in 2011 from the early Toarcian of Strawberry Bank, Ilminster, England.
In Hauffiopteryx, the fibula, or rear shin bone, is significantly larger than the tibia, or front shin bone.
The parent group of Hauffiopteryx is Neoichthyosauria.
Hauffiopteryx is classified in the class Reptilia.

Researchers found that Hauffiopteryx could be either a basal member of Eurhinosauria or a basal member of Thunnosauria, equivalent to the most basal member of Stenopterygiidae excluding Ichthyosaurus.
Hauffiopteryx fossils from Germany and Luxembourg date to the early Toarcian stage of the Early Jurassic, between approximately 182.7 and 181.8 million years ago.
Specimens have been found in Holzmaden, Germany, and Dudelange, Luxembourg.
It lived during the early Toarcian of the Early Jurassic, approximately 182 million years ago, in the Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden.
In Hauffiopteryx altera, the highest points of the upper jaw are located behind the nostrils, whereas in H. typicus they are located beneath them.
The lacrimal bones differ between species: they are triradiate in H. typicus but massive and triangular in H. altera.
